With first and maybe second generation consumer devices? Quite possibly.

As an owner of a Vive, there are several downsides: It fogs up when you first put it on, it has minor screen-door effect (compared to the Oculus DKs), the tether suuuucks (new one less, but still sucks), it is a little heavier than I would like, the (old) strap is difficult, you need an expensive PC, etc etc.

From what Gabe Newell has said about the Gen 2 devices (sounds like 2018), they will: Address the tether issue with wireless (there are going to be wireless accessories on the market starting in ~Q2 2017), and fix the SDE with panels designed for VR. I believe they have a new strap that works better, and they may still be able to improve it; especially if the headset is lighter.

The needing an expensive PC problem will be solved with time; as it stands now you need a high-end i5 (prices will hopefully drop with Ryzen) and at least an RX 470/480. Prices for a PC that will run VR have dropped since the headsets release; processor costs have gone down (for a CPU that meets the minimum requirement) and you no longer need a GTX970 or R9 390X/Fury.

The cost of the headsets will also go down with time; look at computers. Computers used to cost thousands, now they cost hundreds (and smartphones start in the $30 range). Accounting for inflation, that gap is even larger. Yes, the best headset will always be expensive; but you don't always need the best. More headsets are coming out from Oculus, Valve, and other companies, which will create more competition.

The current VR headsets are like the first-gen iPhone or first-gen iPod. In 3-5 years, we will be looking back and going "How did we ever live with that?" "Wow that was an obvious flaw in hindsight!" etc etc. They seem bulky, expensive, and impractical now, but I don't see them going away anytime soon. There are massive groups supporting VR: Khronos, Valve, Facebook/Oculus, Microsoft, Google (although part of it is sucky smartphone VR. Smartphone VR is nothing like PC VR), Sony, and several others.

In the end, if I hadn't used a headset (or had only used a DK1/DK2 or phone VR), I might agree that it isn't going anywhere. The high-end stuff, however, is absolutely amazing. Once the prices fall (As they do with time and competition), we will see much wider adoption. I'm not saying it will be the next iPhone or iPod, but it will probably be very popular amongst gamers. I could definitely see the next generation of consoles (in 202x) being designed for VR, as well as Valve possibly trying to market the Steam Machines/Steam Boxes as high-end no-hassle VR systems.
